[19] In light of the New Delhi High Court's decision, the Canadian Federal Court of Appeal decision of Tretsetsang provides some guidance on the application of Williams for Tibetan claimants:
We agree that the test for determining whether a claimant has a "country of nationality" is the control test as set out in Williams. We also agree that the onus is on the appellant to establish the existence of the asserted impediment and that it would result in the appellant not having the power of control whether India will recognize him as a citizen of India and provide state protection to him. In our view, a country of nationality includes a country where the claimant is a citizen and where the claimant may face an insignificant or minor impediment to accessing state protection from that country but may not include a country where the claimant is a citizen and faces a significant impediment to accessing state protection from that country.

[20] The Federal Court of Appeal in Tretsetsang further outlined the requirements a claimant must meet to demonstrate whether he or she would be able to acquire citizenship:
[A] claimant, who alleges the existence of an impediment to exercise his or her rights of citizenship in a particular country, must establish, on a balance of probabilities:
(a) The existence of a significant impediment that may reasonably be considered capable of preventing the claimant from exercising his or her citizenship rights of state protection in that country of nationality; and
(b) That the claimant has made reasonable efforts to overcome such impediment and that such efforts were unsuccessful such that the claimant was unable to obtain the protection of that state.
What will constitute reasonable efforts to overcome a significant impediment (that has been established by any particular claimant) in any particular situation can only be determined on a case-by-case basis. A claimant will not be obligated to make any effort to overcome such impediment if that claimant establishes that it would not be reasonable to require such claimant to make any such effort.7

[21] The Panel considered the claimants' allegations in light of the requirements in Tretsetsang. The analysis is below.
Omission of principal claimant's first Indian passport application in XXXX 2017

[22] The principal claimant indicated that she made three Indian passport applications, in an attempt to acquire Indian citizenship. The principal claimant explained that she made a paper passport application while she was in Switzerland, at the end of XXXX 2017. The principal claimant allegedly mailed out the paper application to a relative in India, and asked him to deliver the application in person. She explained that the Indian passport office refused to accept the application and did not provide a reason. She further explained that no refusal letter was issued, because the refusal was given orally and passport applications made by Tibetans are not accepted.

[23] The principal claimant's Basis of Claim (BOC) did not mention that she attempted to make an Indian passport application prior to coming to Canada. The Panel asked the principal claimant why she did not indicate that she had in fact attempted to make a passport application before coming to Canada. The principal claimant indicated that she did not know she had to write it in her narrative.

The Panel notes that the lawyer did not indicate that it would be impossible or even unlikely that the principal claimant would be able to have this discrepancy corrected, but only that she might have some difficulties. REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX, the principal claimant, XXXX XXXX, the first minor claimant, and XXXX XXXX, the second minor claimant, claim to be citizens of the People's Republic of China and request protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1
[2] The principal claimant was appointed to be the designated representative for the minor claimants.

[3] The claims were joined in accordance with Rule 55 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules.
ALLEGATIONS
[4] The claimants alleges to fear persecution in China and in India because of their Tibetan ethnicity.
[5] The principal claimant and her husband were both born in India. Their children, the minor claimants are also born in India.

[6] The principal claimant worked for the XXXX XXXX XXXX in India in 2007. During the years that the claimants lived in India, the principal claimant's husband was extorted for money by insurgency groups while working as a XXXX XXXX. The principal claimant alleges that their family were subjected to threats and demands for money at this time. The threats of harm became so severe, that the claimants transferred to Switzerland to work at the XXXX XXXX XXXX in 2014.
[7] The claimants allege that they were advised that they would not be granted refugee status in Switzerland because they were not born in Tibet.

[8] Eventually, the claimants left Switzerland and came to Canada in XXXX 2017 on Canadian visas. The principal claimant's husband remained in Switzerland. The claimants made their refugee claim shortly afterward.
ISSUES

[9] The determinative issues in the claim are countries of reference (China and India), the claimants' national identity regarding their ability to acquire citizenship in India, and credibility.
DETERMINATION

[10] The Panel finds that the claimants are neither Convention Refugees nor are they persons in need of protection.
IDENTITY
Personal identity

[11] In support of their personal identity, the claimants provided copies of their Tibetan Green books and identity certificates indicating that they were born in India.2 On a balance of probabilities, the Panel finds that the claimants are ethnically Tibetan and born on a Tibetan settlement in India as they allege, and accepts their personal identities.
National Identity: whether the claimants be required to show reasonable efforts to acquire citizenship in India

[12] If India is a potential country of reference, then the claimants would also be required to show that they would face a serious possibility of persecution in India, or that on a balance of probabilities, they would be subjected to a danger of torture, or to a risk to life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
[13] In this case, the Panel considered the citizenship laws in India, in light of the recent Federal Court case law regarding Tibetans and their ability to acquire citizenship in India.

[14] The Panel cites the relevant section 3(1) of India's Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003:
Except as provided by sub-section (2), every person born in India,
(a) on or after the 26th day of January, 1950, but before the 1st day of July, 1987;
(b) on or after the 1st day of July, 1987, but before the commencement of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003 and either of whose parents is a citizen of India at the time of his birth;
(c) on or after the commencement of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003, where
(i) both of his parents are citizens of India; or
(ii) one of whose parents is a citizen of India and the other is not an illegal migrant at the time of his birth, shall be a citizen of India by birth. [italics added]3

[15] Therefore, according to section 3 (1) (a), if the principal claimant's date of birth falls between January 26, 1950 and before July 1, 1987, and she was born in India, then she falls under one of the categories allowing her to have Indian citizenship. Given that the principal claimant was born in India on XXXX XXXX, 1977, the principal claimant meets this criteria, and should be granted citizenship on this basis. The minor claimants, who are born in India after July 1, 1987, would meet the criteria in accordance with section 3 (1) (b), cited above.

[16] Nonetheless, the Panel is cognizant of the past difficulties that Tibetans living in India have experienced in being recognized as citizens, despite the existence of this law. However, in recent years, there have been some developments in the law, leading more Tibetans to be recognized as citizens in India.

[17] According to the leading Federal Court of Appeal case of Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Williams, a claimant cannot be granted refugee protection if he has citizenship available to him in another safe country and it is within his power to acquire citizenship.4 The burden of proof lies on the claimant himself to demonstrate otherwise.

[18] According to the September 22, 2016 decision of the Delhi High Court, "the nationality of Tibetans born in India between 1950 and 1987 cannot be questioned under the Citizenship Act" in response to petitions filed by three Tibetans born in India, who attempted to apply for Indian passports.5 The High Court directed the Ministry of External Affairs and all passport-issuing authorities to process applications for passports of eligible Tibetan refugees, or else be held in contempt of court.6

[19] In light of the New Delhi High Court's decision, the Canadian Federal Court of Appeal decision of Tretsetsang provides some guidance on the application of Williams for Tibetan claimants:
We agree that the test for determining whether a claimant has a "country of nationality" is the control test as set out in Williams. We also agree that the onus is on the appellant to establish the existence of the asserted impediment and that it would result in the appellant not having the power of control whether India will recognize him as a citizen of India and provide state protection to him. In our view, a country of nationality includes a country where the claimant is a citizen and where the claimant may face an insignificant or minor impediment to accessing state protection from that country but may not include a country where the claimant is a citizen and faces a significant impediment to accessing state protection from that country.

[20] The Federal Court of Appeal in Tretsetsang further outlined the requirements a claimant must meet to demonstrate whether he or she would be able to acquire citizenship:
[A] claimant, who alleges the existence of an impediment to exercise his or her rights of citizenship in a particular country, must establish, on a balance of probabilities:
(a) The existence of a significant impediment that may reasonably be considered capable of preventing the claimant from exercising his or her citizenship rights of state protection in that country of nationality; and
(b) That the claimant has made reasonable efforts to overcome such impediment and that such efforts were unsuccessful such that the claimant was unable to obtain the protection of that state.
What will constitute reasonable efforts to overcome a significant impediment (that has been established by any particular claimant) in any particular situation can only be determined on a case-by-case basis. A claimant will not be obligated to make any effort to overcome such impediment if that claimant establishes that it would not be reasonable to require such claimant to make any such effort.7

[21] The Panel considered the claimants' allegations in light of the requirements in Tretsetsang. The analysis is below.
Omission of principal claimant's first Indian passport application in XXXX 2017

[22] The principal claimant indicated that she made three Indian passport applications, in an attempt to acquire Indian citizenship. The principal claimant explained that she made a paper passport application while she was in Switzerland, at the end of XXXX 2017. The principal claimant allegedly mailed out the paper application to a relative in India, and asked him to deliver the application in person. She explained that the Indian passport office refused to accept the application and did not provide a reason. She further explained that no refusal letter was issued, because the refusal was given orally and passport applications made by Tibetans are not accepted.

[23] The principal claimant's Basis of Claim (BOC) did not mention that she attempted to make an Indian passport application prior to coming to Canada. The Panel asked the principal claimant why she did not indicate that she had in fact attempted to make a passport application before coming to Canada. The principal claimant indicated that she did not know she had to write it in her narrative.

[24] The Panel does not find that this is a satisfactory explanation for the omission. The principal claimant is represented by counsel and was assisted by counsel at the time she prepared her BOC. This application allegedly took place right before she left for Canada. Given the nature of the claim, and given that India is a proposed country of reference, the Panel finds that this is a significant omission. The Panel asked the claimant whether she had a supporting letter from her relative who allegedly tried to submit her Indian passport application on her behalf in India. The principal claimant indicated that she did not have such a document, as their conversation took place over the phone.

[25] Without any documentation of the XXXX 2017 passport application being made or refused, along with the omission from the BOC, the Panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the principal claimant did not make a passport application in XXXX 2017, and she has attempted to embellish her efforts to obtain Indian citizenship and to overcome any impediments to this process.
Principal claimant's efforts to make an Indian passport application on XXXX XXXX, 2017 and XXXX XXXX, 2018 do not present significant impediment

[26] The principal claimant provided two print-outs of her Indian passport applications which she made after arriving in Canada and making her refugee claim. The first one is a paper application, completed on XXXX XXXX, 2017.8 The second passport application was completed online on XXXX XXXX, 2018, a week before the hearing.9 The principal claimant provided an affidavit from a friend who accompanied her to the Indian consulate in Canada, which indicated that the passport application was refused at the counter.

[27] The principal claimant did not have any documentation of a refusal from the Indian consulate, or any response from the Indian consulate, confirming that her passport application would not be accepted for consideration. The principal claimant explained that her passport application was refused by the passport clerk, and so it was not be considered by the Indian passport-issuing authorities. She was advised by this clerk to contact the Indian Consulate. The principal claimant indicated that this was the impediment that prevented her from having her application considered.

[28] The principal claimant provided copies of emails sent to the Indian consulate to follow up on how she could make a passport application.10 The last email was sent in XXXX 2017.11 In the two emails, the principal claimant does not mention that she attempted to make an Indian passport application and that the clerk had refused to take it. The emails themselves are brief and general in content, simply asking for information about the Indian passport application process for Tibetans. The Panel finds that these emails lack probative value, in demonstrating the principal claimant's efforts to follow up on the refusal of her passport application by the passport clerk, and they are given no weight in corroborating the principal claimant's attempts to overcome the impediment to her passport application.

[29] The principal claimant provided a print-out of her online Indian passport application form, which was completed on XXXX XXXX, 2018.12 There is no indication that this form was submitted, or that this form was refused by the Indian government authorities. At the time of the hearing, this application would have been completed ten days before the hearing. The principal claimant indicated that she had some technical difficulties filling out the form, but was able to do so eventually. The Panel finds that this is not a significant impediment to the application process. There is no indication that this application form will not be accepted by the Indian government in the future.
Husband's attempts to obtain an Indian passport are given no weight

[30] The principal claimant also provided an affidavit from her husband's friend, which indicates that her husband attempted to make an Indian passport application in Switzerland, and the application form was refused by the passport clerk on XXXX XXXX, 2018, that the Indian Consulate would not accept passport applications unless it received an official order form the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA).13

[31] However, according to the documentary evidence, the MEA has already issued a new policy in March 2017, to all passport offices in India and abroad to process pending applications of Tibetan Refugee applicants born in India between January 26, 1950 and July 1, 1987.14 The principal claimant's husband was born XXXX XXXX, 1974, and falls in this category. It is uncertain then why a passport clerk in Switzerland would refuse the husband's application pending an order that has already been issued by the MEA.

[32] Furthermore, the Panel finds that there is no documentation from the principal claimant's husband himself that this 2018 passport application attempt took place, or why he made the decision to file a passport application a month before the claimants' hearing. The witness statement provided on behalf of the husband is second-hand information, and therefore has less probative value to the claim, and it is given no weight.

[33] However, the husband did provide an affidavit indicating that he attempted to submit an Indian passport application in India, on XXXX XXXX, 2016 and his application was also refused at that time.15 The Panel is not required to evaluate the efforts made by the principal claimant's husband to obtain Indian citizenship, as he is not a claimant to this proceeding. The Panel can only consider the husband's attempts, as it relates to the principal claimant's efforts to acquire Indian citizenship, as a similarly situated person. There is no indication regarding how the husband attempted to overcome this impediment when his passport application was allegedly refused in 2016, and so once again, this affidavit is given no weight in light of the claimants' allegations.
Principal claimant's attempts to acquire Indian citizenship does not demonstrate a significant impediment, and principal claimant has not made reasonable efforts to overcome these impediments

[34] In summary, the principal claimant alleges that passport clerks in India, Canada and Switzerland have all refused to accept passport application forms from Tibetans. The passport clerks at local Indian consulate offices do not have the authority to issue or deny passports.

[35] As indicated above, the Indian High Court has already directed the Ministry of External Affairs and all passport-issuing authorities to process applications for passports of eligible Tibetan refugees, or else be held in contempt of court.16 The documentary evidence is silent on the prevalence of passport office clerks at Indian consulates globally refusing to accept application forms for the Indian government to consider, and risking themselves to be held in contempt of the court order.

[36] The principal claimant herself has not attempted to formally litigate her matter, in light of the fact that her Indian passport application has been allegedly refused by passport clerks at two offices, in two different countries. When asked about whether she would consider litigating the matter, the principal claimant did not answer the question directly, and simply indicated that she needed to be living in India for one year before applying for citizenship.

[37] The Panel takes into account the already existing credibly concerns with the principal claimant's as stated above. The Panel also considers the fact that there has been no formal refusal from any Indian government official for the principal claimant's passport applications. The Panel finds on a balance of probabilities, that the principal claimant has not received an official response from the Indian government with the issuing authority, refusing her latest passport application. The Panel finds that refusal by a passport clerk is not a significant impediment for the reasons given above. Therefore, the Panel finds on a balance of probabilities, that the principal claimant has failed to demonstrate that a significant impediment has occurred to prevent her Indian passport application from being processed, and she has not made reasonable efforts to overcome these impediments.
Opinion evidence of lawyer identifies impediments to the principal claimant's ability to acquire citizenship

[38] The principal claimant provided an eighteen page legal opinion letter from a lawyer in India, who represented successful Tibetan litigants in obtaining their Indian passports. In the letter, the lawyer indicated that he was asked to provide a legal opinion on whether the principal claimant was likely to be eligible for Indian citizenship. Thirteen pages of this opinion letter summarize the law under the Indian Citizenship Act, and only a portion of the letter is specific to the principal claimant's situation. The lawyer concludes, based on the identity documents submitted to him by the principal claimant, that she would likely not be able to acquire citizenship, under sections 3 and 5 of the Indian Citizenship Act.

[39] However, upon closer examination of the letter, the lawyer indicates that the principal claimant has a Matriculation Certificate, which is one of the documents accepted by the Indian passport office.17 However, there is a discrepancy in her day of birth on the Matriculation Certificate and her identity certificate and registration certificate. The lawyer recommends that the principal claimant should have the Matriculation certificate corrected, but that she might have some difficulties doing so, and this might affect her ability to apply for a passport. The Panel notes that the lawyer did not indicate that it would be impossible or even unlikely that the principal claimant would be able to have this discrepancy corrected, but only that she might have some difficulties. The Panel does not find this to be a significant impediment to the principal claimant's ability to acquire this document, if this is required for her passport application, and the principal claimant has not provided reasons why she would be unable to correct the discrepancy in her documents.

[40] The lawyer also indicates that the principal claimant may be unlikely to succeed in obtaining Indian citizenship, because she is currently out of the country.18 The lawyer indicates that the principal claimant must be residing in India for one year before making her passport application. The Panel asked the principal claimant why she could not return to India, live there for one full year, and then make her passport application. The principal claimant indicated that she had not renewed her Registration Certificate, as she is required to do so, every six months in order to continue living in India legally.

[41] Once again, the Panel does not find the requirement of living in India for a full year before making a passport application, to be a significant impediment. The principal claimant had lived in India since birth, and only left the country in 2014 for Switzerland, to accompany her husband on his work permit. The principal claimant then left for Canada a year after living in Switzerland. The principal claimant's identity certificate indicates she obtained a "no objection to return", valid for ten years.19 She has not been out of the country for ten years, as she left India in 2014. The minor claimants' identity certificates indicate that they are permitted to be out of the country until XXXX XXXX, 2020.20

[42] According to the documentary evidence, all Tibetans traveling on an Identity Certificate must have a No Objection to Return to India Certificate (NORI) in order to re-enter India.21 NORIs are issued to Tibetans who have received approval to exit India. In addition, Tibetans must also obtain a return visa from the Indian Embassy.22 This visa is at the discretion of the Indian authorities. The claimants have permission from the Indian government to be out of the country for the current time period that they have been absent from India.

[43] Applicants for a return visa must submit an online visa application and bring their physical copy of their application along with a number of supporting documents.23 The documentary evidence indicates that Tibetans simply require a valid NORI, a return visa issued by an Indian embassy, and a valid Identity Certificate in order to legally return to India. Despite the fact that return visas are discretionary, the claimants' travel documents are all valid. The claimants only need to obtain a return visa from the Indian embassy. The principal claimant has not indicated that she would be unable to obtain a return visa.

[44] It also came to the Panel's attention at the end of the hearing that the last page of the principal claimant's Registration Certificate indicates that her Residential Permit has been extended up to XXXX XXXX, 2019.24 Therefore, it is unclear why the principal claimant believes that she cannot return, as her Registration Certificate is not yet expired. Even if the principal claimant had an expired Registration Certificate, the Panel finds that the principal claimant's belief that she would not be able to return to India, is based on speculation. According to the documentary evidence, the Central Tibetan Administration has indicated that those who do not renew their Registration Certificate before the expiration, may be denied renewal, although sometimes renewals are sometimes still granted on humanitarian grounds.25

[45] Therefore, it is at the discretion of the Foreign Registration Office, whether or not an expired Registration Certificate can still be renewed. The Panel finds that even if the principal claimant had an expired Registration Certificate, she has not demonstrated that this would be a significant impediment to her ability to return to India, attempt to renew her Registration Certificate, and to obtain citizenship.

[46] The Panel also takes into account that the principal claimant has not met with this lawyer in person for a consultation to explain her situation. Therefore, it is uncertain what information this lawyer had, other than paper copies of her identity documents. This opinion letter is based solely on the identity documents provided to him.

[47] The Panel finds on a balance of probabilities, that it is within the claimants' control to acquire citizenship in India and the claimants have not met their onus to show otherwise. It is the principal claimant's personal decision whether or not she wishes to make reasonable efforts to acquire citizenship and to seek the protection of the state.

[48] Therefore, given the above findings, the Panel finds on a balance of probabilities that India is a country of reference.
India is a country of reference: there is no well-founded fear of persecution in India

[49] The principal claimant indicated that she feared that she would be deported to Tibet if she returned to China, because she has been unable to renew her Registration Certificate, which provides her with the right to legally reside in India as a Tibetan.

[50] For the reasons above, the Panel finds that the principal claimant's belief that she would not be able to return to India based on an allegedly expired Registration Certificate is based on speculation. Furthermore, according to the documentary evidence, Tibetans are never actually forced to leave India, nor are they handed over to the Chinese authorities.26 Therefore, the Panel finds that the principal claimant's belief that she would be deported to Tibet if her Registration Certificate is not renewed, is not a well-founded fear of persecution.

[51] The principal claimant mentioned in her BOC that her family had been subjected to extortion by anti-Tibetan insurgency groups in India, as a result of her husband's work with the XXXX XXXX XXXX. She did not mention this initially, when asked to explain whether she feared returning to India. When the Panel asked the principal claimant whether this was also a reason why she believed she could not return to India, the principal claimant indicated that this was a very stressful time for her family. The principal claimant did not provide a direct response when she was asked whether she was ever personally targeted by these groups. She simply indicated that her family received the threats.

[52] These extortion allegations are primarily concerned with the principal claimant's husband's work. Once again, the husband is not a claimant to this proceeding, and is unable to explain these allegations in greater detail. There is no indication in the principal claimant's BOC whether these groups had ever targeted the family after 2012. The husband had returned to India in 2016 to allegedly make his passport application, and there was no noted incident of persecution by any such groups in his affidavit upon his return.27

[53] Moreover, the claimants moved to Switzerland in 2014. They remained there until XXXX XXXX, 2017. The husband remains in Switzerland on a work permit. The principal claimant explained that her husband decided to remain in Switzerland, rather than joining the claimants in making a refugee claim, because the husband has responsibilities to the Central Tibetan Administration in India, and has to return to India eventually. The principal claimant indicated that they did not make a refugee claim in Switzerland, because she did not believe she had a right to ask for refugee protection, given that her husband was there for work-related purposes.

[54] The Panel finds that this is not a reasonable explanation for failing to claim in Switzerland. The principal claimant is an educated person, and was able to learn about the Canadian refugee claim process at the time that she did, and to seek legal advice on her Canadian refugee claim. The Panel finds that in the time span of over two years that she was living in Switzerland, the principal claimant had every opportunity to make a refugee claim. The Panel finds that this shows a lack of subjective fear, and draws a negative inference to the credibility of her allegations, regarding her fear of returning to India.

[55] Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, the Panel finds that the claimants will not be persecuted upon their return to India, and they have not established that they have a well-founded fear of persecution if they return to India, or that on a balance of probabilities, they would be subjected to a danger of torture, or to a risk to life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
CONCLUSION

[56] After carefully considering all the evidence in this claim, and for the reasons above, the Panel finds that the claimants are not Convention refugees under section 96 of the IRPA nor are they persons in need of protection under subsection 97 of the IRPA.

[57] Therefore, the claims are rejected.
